doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Father's break with Castro and wanting to leave Cuba
summary: His father turned against the revolution; youths persecuted for Beatles music made him want to leave.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: All right. So leading up to the Mariel boatlift, was there a period of a number of years where you started to think I really am unhappy here, I want to pursue this music career but it’s not going to happen here. I mean what was your motivation to come to the States in such a manner that you did?

I always, Monk, since I started using my mind, I’m also I have to say that my dad, who was a huge Fidel Castro fan up to the point that my father fought on Bay of Pigs defending the Cuban regime. In 1965 he broke ties with the revolution because he started seeing that Castro’s promises — that everything was like a lie. He thought that Castro
was a liar, that he was not doing what he promised from the beginning, so he broke ties with the revolution and

with the Cuban government. And that in a sense helped me out to determine the different direction. But another musical event, before my father broke ties with the government, that was a musical thing that made me decide that living in Cuba under that regime was not for me. And that was when I started seeing that young people, the youth in Cuba that used to like the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, started to be prosecuted and that we were at parties listening and dancing to the Beatles with no drugs, no amount of alcohol. We were just 14, 15, 16, 17, young guys. And we were dancing through the, with the music [sings] All you need is love. And the police will appear and stop the party and then one of the guys might start an argument with the policeman and then that guy was taken to jail, then later they started taking a bunch of people to jail and started cutting their hairs and cutting their tight pants. And I remember I told my father if this revolution is afraid of four guys with long hair, three guitars and a drums this thing is not solid. So that was the beginning. So to make a long story short since I was I would say twelve or thirteen years old I wanted to leave that place. I knew that Cuba was not for me. And the other thing, Cuba was not for me because one of the things I have never been able to incorporate into my personality into my life is something very near it, in life, for some people, which is hypocrisy. I cannot behave [gap] demonstrate to you, “Oh yeah, loyalty for Fidel, oh yeah, Communism.” And then when I get a chance defect. I always was straightforward. I always expressed what I liked, and that got me into a lot of trouble. It have got me along the way because I grew up — right now I’m 68 years old and I have found through life that on numerous occasions telling the truth got you consequences. But in the case of Cuba, yes, since I was like thirteen years old I wanted to leave, but I didn’t have the opportunity of doing so.
